Every time, I see Ryan teaching with great passion; I really want to talk to him, so I’ve started reading the books he has written.

Week Project:
After discussing birds and technology this week, a thought has lingered in my mind: when we use various devices to record birds in flight, what exactly are we seeing?
Take Étienne-Jules Marey, mentioned in class, as an example: he broke down the process of bird flight into a series of sequential images, making rapid wingbeats—normally difficult for the naked eye to discern—clearly visible. Yet, this mode of observation has its limitations: if we focus solely on wing movements and flight patterns, we risk overlooking the wind, the surrounding environment, and the reasons “why”the bird is flying the way it is.
I do not mean to dismiss the value of data. Positional data and flight trajectories help us uncover details that might otherwise go unnoticed. The problem, however, is that once we hold a clear map of a flight path, we are prone to the illusion that we have "fully understood" the bird. Yet, knowing “where” a bird turns is vastly different from knowing “why” it turns. The same turning maneuver could be linked to varying weather conditions or simply to the bird’s search for food; a trajectory alone cannot reveal these underlying causes.
This also piqued my interest in Ryan’s explanation of “ornithomancy” (divination by birds). As I understood the lecture, the belief system involved posits that deities reside in the sky—realms inaccessible to direct human sight or approach—whereas birds possess the ability to ascend into the heavens. Consequently, birds were viewed as messengers bridging the human and divine worlds, with people seeking to decipher the will of the gods by observing avian behavior. Their role as this medium is inextricably linked to their capacity for flight and to human conceptions of the sky.
It is fascinating to juxtapose these two modes of observation: while both involve watching birds in flight, the observers are looking for entirely different things. One approach seeks to interpret divine will through the bird's behavior, while the other analyzes the mechanics of flight by breaking down the movement. Because their objectives and premises differ, they draw attention to different aspects of the bird. Ultimately, what we see depends not only on the bird itself but also on our observational intent and the methods used to record it. This realization has taught me that clearly seeing one aspect of a bird does not equate to understanding it in its entirety.
results_discussion:
datafication results in divination and divination results from datafication
Continuing from last week: the digital mindset—breaking things down into small chunks, storing them, and recombining them—predates digital technology. This week, we look at bird flight, one of the earliest phenomena to be "broken down into small chunks" in this way.
We conclude with the concept of the swarm (or flock/murmuration): a model where simple rules give rise to complex collective behavior—a concept that has migrated from the realm of animation into military applications.Marey’s chronophotographic gun (1882)—Tatin argued that the subject of study should not be the bird itself but "flight" itself: stripping the action away from the animal to arrive at a purely mathematical solution. It featured two clockwork mechanisms—one to advance the film and the other to adjust the aperture—linking the device to the lineage of automata and robots.
William Kentridge-A South African artist known for depicting birds and flight; created an animated accompaniment for Schubert’s *Winterreise* (specifically the song "Die Krähe" / "The Crow"); currently holding a major exhibition at the Goodman Gallery in London.
Pierre Belon, *History of the Nature of Birds* (1555): One of the earliest works of comparative anatomy, featuring side-by-side illustrations of bird and human skeletons—revealing the human within the bird and the bird within the human. This concept of "structural analogy" served as the starting point for all subsequent biomimicry.
Leonardo da Vinci: *Codex on the Flight of Birds* (1505–06); he created mechanical bird props for theatrical productions and designed the "Exploding Cart" for the Florentine Easter celebration (in which a mechanical dove would swoop down from a height to ignite fireworks, serving as a harvest omen). His sketches functioned as "scientific slices" captured from dynamic processes, intended to enable replication.
Borelli, *On the Movement of Animals* (1734): Used geometric diagrams to link animal movements with human anatomy; his analysis of birds was applied to the development of increasingly complex automata.
Islamic Automata: Al-Jazari’s *Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices* (c. 1200) featured water- or air-powered mechanical birds and golden trees; this knowledge reached Europe via the libraries of Toledo and Córdoba. James Cox created a piece modeled on the Byzantine throne (presented to Catherine the Great; now housed in the Hermitage Museum).
The Pinnacle of 18th-Century Automata: Merlin’s *Silver Swan* (1773); Vaucanson’s mechanical duck and automatic loom (utilizing punched cards—the precursors to modern computers).
Key Insight: The earliest creators of mechanical birds already grasped that intelligence is not exclusive to humans or to a single individual; rather, it exists within multi-component systems.
Cybernetics: From Flocks to Systems
Non-human collective intelligence is ubiquitous in nature—seen in insects, fish, and birds. "All parts act as one, moving in unison."
Post-WWII Macy Conferences → Cybernetics. The title of Norbert Wiener’s 1948 book says it all: *Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine*—placing humans, animals, and machines within the same framework.
Example (cited by the lecturer): A home thermostat. It turns on the heat when the temperature drops below 20°C and shuts it off once that temperature is reached; the system maintains its own balance—a state known as *homeostasis*. No single entity is making the decision; rather, the system is self-regulating.
Systems Theory (originating in 1930s biology): One cannot study a single stone or fish in a river in isolation; one must consider the entire river—its forces, chemistry, and the network of species interactions.
The result: Humans, animals, and machines are all parts of a larger system, interconnected by feedback loops.
3. Mechanical Animals in the Laboratory
After 1948, laboratory-created mechanical animals proliferated: Wiener’s light-sensitive mechanical moth, Grey Walter’s electromechanical tortoise, von Neumann’s self-replicating automata, and Shannon’s maze-solving mechanical mouse (Shannon also conducted long-term research on communication among ants and bees). The goal was to understand the nature of intelligence and information by interpreting collective behavior and movement—and then to apply that knowledge to fields such as commerce, warfare, environmental science, and cognitive studies.
4. The ICARUS Project: Satellite Divination
Based at the Max Planck Institute in Berlin, ICARUS stands for "International Cooperation for Animal Research Using Space" and is set to relaunch in 2025. It uses satellites to track animal migration, involving 10.6 billion positioning sensors, 8.9 million records, nearly 2,000 species, and close to 6,000 data contributors.
Beyond tracking migration routes and disease, the project aims to "predict ecological changes and natural disasters"—a practice the lecturer calls "digital ornithomancy." It brings data-driven analysis into the realm of predicting the collective future for species across the entire globe. Vladan Joler, Gordan Savičić, and Felix Stalder, *Infrastructure of a Migratory Bird* (2022): A zoomable data map—ranging from the scale of insects to that of the planet—that charts the relationships between social, technical, informational, and ecological elements surrounding a rewilding project for the Northern Bald Ibis. In their own words, this bird "flies not only through the air but also through data"—much like Marey’s bird. URL: latentspaces.zhdk.ch/imb/
Heba Y. Amin, *As Birds Flying*: In 2013, a stork equipped with a scientific tracker was detained by Egyptian officials who mistook it for a piece of espionage equipment; the artwork explores surveillance, paranoia, and the migration patterns of both birds and humans from the bird's perspective.
AeroVironment Nano Hummingbird drone (2011, DARPA); bird-shaped surveillance drones have seen a resurgence in the 2020s.
5. Boids Algorithm → Swarm Warfare
Craig Reynolds, *Flocks, Herds and Schools* (SIGGRAPH 1987): A simulation of bird flocks created for computer animation, based on three rules—separation, cohesion, and alignment (the lecture notes mistakenly used "integration"). Simple rules lead to complex emergent behavior. This work influenced animation, autonomous driving, military swarm robotics, and social network modeling.
Military adaptation: The 1997 RAND report *Swarming and the Future of Conflict* by Arquilla and Ronfeldt proposed the concept of "swarm warfare." While the US military did not adopt it at the time, resource-poor adversaries did: Ukraine and Iran have used swarms of low-cost drones to counter the expensive weaponry of Russia and the US—a form of asymmetric warfare.
Why it works: Swarms overwhelm human perception—countless small movements coalesce into a shapeless whole that the human eye cannot track, thereby creating a "fog of war."
Key takeaway: The roots of this swarm model lie in 19th-century physics' attempts to predict dynamic systems combined with late-20th-century computer animation. The very algorithms you use for animation are now redrawing the geopolitical map.
6. Phractyl Macrobat
The Macrobat is a bird-like, bipedal helicopter designed by the South African company Phractyl for executives to bypass traffic congestion in African cities; it features bird-leg-style landing gear and performs "near-vertical" takeoffs and landings. Currently, only CGI demonstrations exist. The lecturer juxtaposes this with a 1555 illustration by Belon comparing human and avian skeletal structures: five centuries later, the fantasy of human-avian structural fusion has transformed into a luxury commuting vehicle.
7. Conclusion + Q&A
A 3,000-year lineage: Hittite divination → Archytas → al-Jazari → Da Vinci/Borelli/Belon → Marey → Kentridge → Arquilla & Ronfeldt → Macrobat. Each step follows the pattern: "deconstructing animal movement → interpreting it → predicting or replicating it."
The lecturer acknowledges that this is a "highly simplified" account of complex relationships. The "Morning Song" (interpreting birdsong) represents the earliest instance of humans misreading birds; ICARUS, conversely, represents a correct reading—migratory birds serve as the "canaries in the coal mine" for our ecological future, and with terrifying accuracy.
A student asks: Is this the same thing as the Chinese practice of divination based on falling leaves? The lecturer: I completely agree; both East and West share the practice of translating an unknowable future into readable symbols.
title: Asuka's Divination and Data Theory
introduction: For 3,000 years, humans have interpreted birds—first to read divine will, then to turn flight into data, and now to predict climate and coordinate drones. The teacher claims that datafication is just divination in modern dress.
